**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I sit here, staring at the blank page, the cursor blinking like a metronome counting down the seconds of my indecision. A thousand words—what a strange, arbitrary number. It feels like both too much and not enough. Too much because the mind is a cluttered attic, and sifting through the dust for something worth saying is exhausting. Not enough because the moment you start, the words spill out like water from a cracked dam, and suddenly, a thousand feels like a prison.

I think about the things that haunt me. The way the light slants through the window in the late afternoon, turning the air golden and thick, like honey. The way my grandmother’s hands looked when she peeled oranges, her fingers stained with citrus, the scent lingering long after the fruit was gone. Small things. Insignificant things. And yet, they are the anchors that keep me from drifting too far.

There’s a quote I love—*“The world is full of magic things, patiently waiting for our senses to grow sharper.”* I don’t know who said it, but it feels true. We move through life half-asleep, bumping into miracles without noticing. The way a stranger’s laughter can lift your mood. The way rain sounds different depending on the surface it hits—roofs, leaves, pavement, skin. The way a book can feel like a friend, its pages worn from too many readings, its spine creased from being carried everywhere.

I wonder if we’re all just stories in the end. Not the grand, epic kind, but the quiet, messy ones. The kind where the hero doesn’t slay a dragon but instead learns to live with the burn of heartbreak. The kind where the villain is just loneliness, and the battle is fought in the silence of 3 a.m. The kind where the happy ending isn’t a wedding or a victory but a single moment of peace—sitting on a porch, drinking bad coffee, watching the sunrise like it’s the first time.

I think about time. How it stretches and compresses like taffy. How a single hour can feel like an eternity when you’re waiting for news—good or bad—and how a decade can vanish in the blink of an eye when you’re lost in love or work or grief. We measure our lives in minutes, but we *live* them in moments. The problem is, we never know which moments matter until they’re already memories.

There’s a tree outside my window. I don’t know its name, but it’s old, its branches gnarled and twisting like arthritic fingers. In the spring, it blooms with white flowers that smell like vanilla. In the fall, its leaves turn the color of rust. I’ve watched it through all the seasons, and it occurs to me that it has seen more of my life than most people. It was there when I cried over my first heartbreak. It was there when I stayed up all night writing a story that would never be published. It was there when I sat in the dark, too tired to turn on the light, wondering if any of this—any of *me*—mattered.

Maybe that’s the real magic. Not that we’re here, but that anything *else* is here with us. That the universe, in all its vast, indifferent glory, still bothers to grow trees and paint sunsets and let us taste strawberries. That despite everything, we still find reasons to keep going.

I don’t know if any of this makes sense. Maybe it’s just the rambling of a mind that’s had too much coffee and not enough sleep. But here’s the thing about words—they don’t have to be perfect. They just have to be *true*. And right now, this is my truth: I am here. I am breathing. I am trying. And sometimes, that’s enough.

The cursor blinks. The page is no longer blank. A thousand words, give or take. A thousand little pieces of me, scattered like seeds. Maybe some will take root. Maybe none will. But I planted them anyway.

And that has to count for something.
